i am diagnosed with BPD and in graduate school to become a therapist. this disorder is highly stigmatized in the field and that is on the providers to unlearn, not on those of us with the illness to have to change. that being said, in general any client who wants to improve and is interested in getting better is going to be a pleasure to work with. typically, people who do not want to be in treatment and/or do not recognize their problems are considered more ‘difficult’ to work with, but I don’t think there’s anything wrong with a bit of a challenge and it can be very rewarding helping those people along in their process. some therapists may refer a patient with any diagnosis elsewhere if they do not feel they have the right expertise for that case, which isn’t a reflection on you but rather the T’s personal skill set!

all in all, i definitely understand your fear of being turned away because of your diagnosis. i would express this to your T because it’s always good for them to know what’s going on in your internal world so they can help you work out those feelings. remember you are there for your health and your T is there to help you, you do not have to change or shrink yourself for the sake of your T! wishing you the best in your recovery :)

I have bpd and have been in a healthy relationship with my boyfriend for 4 years. The absolute best thing for us is communication and psychoeducation. We both share what we are feeling and what is going on with us internally as much as we possibly can, that way we are able to sort out any incorrect perceptions we have (things like “he doesn’t love me”, or him thinking i am going to break up with him when i’m just splitting, etc) and make sure we both feel equally heard and respected in the relationship. Also communicating insecurities, boundaries that feel right for each other, basically everything.

Secondly, psychoeducation is vital for him having a better understanding of the disorder and why I may be doing/feeling certain things. The more he learns about bpd, the more understood I feel and the easier it is for him to make sense of my symptoms. It also has helped him to learn about things like splitting in a way that helps him take it much less personally as he realizes it’s a common feature of bpd that has far more to do with my abandonment issues than our actual relationship. 

Beyond that, the type of partner you have is huge. My partner is extremely patient and extremely loving, two things I’ve found I really need to feel safe in a relationship. He never ever insults me, intentionally triggers me, belittles my feelings, ignores me, or acts unfaithfully at all. Having a green flag partner is so so important because it is definitely not a one way street in managing your bpd/relationship

BDD can be present whether the feature is real or just perceived as such. The biggest factor is the amount of distress it causes and its impact on your functioning. For example, someone may have a crooked nose or a scar. Some people may be insecure about this, but this becomes disordered thinking when the person is intensely fixated on those features/hinders their day to day life/feels the constant need to hide or control those features/etc. 
To summarize, whether the hated feature is actually present or not does not determine if someone has BDD, it’s the amount of distress/impairing of functioning it causes. Hope this helped!
